data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Earth's elliptical orbit around the Sun causes seasonal changes in the solar flux received at the top of the atmosphere.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If Earth's orbit were perfectly circular, the heliocentric distance would be constant and orbital eccentricity would not modulate incoming solar radiation.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the Sun emitted a collimated, non-diverging beam of radiation rather than radiating isotropically, the inverse-square law would not apply and distance variations would not alter flux.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Because the Earth's orbital path is elliptical, the Earth-Sun distance varies throughout the year. According to the inverse-square law, the intensity of solar radiation diminishes with the square of the distance. Earth reaches perihelion (closest approach) in early January and aphelion (farthest distance) in early July, resulting in approximately 6.9% more solar flux at perihelion than at aphelion.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
